hints: Separate the variables so that $\sin^2(3y)$ is integrated with respect to $y$ and $4\sec(2x)\tan(2x)$ with respect to $x$.
Use $\sin^2(3y)=\frac12(1-\cos6y)$, and account for the factor $2$ when integrating $\sec(2x)\tan(2x)$.
Apply $y=0$ when $x=\frac\pi6$ to determine the integration constant.
Substitute $y=\frac\pi6$ into the resulting relation and solve for the value of $x$ in $0\leq x<\frac\pi4$, rounding to 3 decimal places.
walkthrough:
Rearrange the differential equation to prepare for separating variables:
$$\cos(2x)\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4\tan(2x)}{\sin^2(3y)}$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4\sec(2x)\tan(2x)}{\sin^2(3y)}$$

Integrate the left-hand side using the half-angle identity $\sin^2(3y) = \dfrac{1}{2}(1 - \cos(6y))$:
$$\int \sin^2(3y)\,\mathrm{d}y = \dfrac{1}{2}\int (1 - \cos(6y))\,\mathrm{d}y = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(y - \dfrac{1}{6}\sin(6y)\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}y - \dfrac{1}{12}\sin(6y)$$

Integrate the right-hand side using $\int \sec(kx)\tan(kx)\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{k}\sec(kx)$:
$$\int 4\sec(2x)\tan(2x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 4\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sec(2x)\right) = 2\sec(2x) + C$$

Equate the two sides to obtain the general solution:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}y - \dfrac{1}{12}\sin(6y) = 2\sec(2x) + C$$

Apply the initial condition $y = 0$ when $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to find $C$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}(0) - \dfrac{1}{12}\sin(0) = 2\sec\left(2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + C$$
$$0 = 2\sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C$$
Since $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies \sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2$:
$$0 = 2(2) + C = 4 + C \implies C = -4$$

Round the final answer correct to 3 decimal places:
$$x = 0.541$$
